q: Why is spontaneous ventilation maintained during rigid bronchoscopy for a foreign body?
o: To avoid pushing the object distally with positive pressure
why: PPV can push the foreign body further down or create ball-valve hyperinflation.

q: Which CXR finding suggests a ball-valve effect?
why: The CXR may also be normal, or show collapse.

q: What dose of lidocaine is sprayed onto the cords via an atomiser before rigid bronchoscopy in a child?
why: Topical lidocaine 4 mg/kg via a MAD reduces airway reactivity while spontaneous ventilation is maintained.

q: Which items are red flags needing immediate removal?
why: Button batteries cause rapid burns and erosion.

q: What dexamethasone dose is given for laryngeal oedema?
How should a choking child over 1 year with an ineffective cough be managed?
why: Under 1 year, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.

q: Which is a bronchial (rather than laryngeal) foreign body sign?
o: Wheeze and reduced breath sounds on one side
why: Laryngeal FBs cause voice change and stridor.

q: What is a major intraoperative risk with TIVA during rigid bronchoscopy?
why: Volatile delivery is unreliable through the open bronchoscope; TIVA needs careful depth control.

q: What is the dose of nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 in croup or post-extubation stridor?
Which is a surgical immediate complication?
o: Loss of the foreign body distally or into the other bronchus
